newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Patten knocks China for "tinkering" with Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Patten knocks China for "tinkering" with Hong Kong.

text.p: Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten attacked the territory's government-in-waiting on Thursday for planning to tinker with Hong Kong's "Rolls Royce" engine and water down democracy when Britain pulls out this year.

Patten's comments, during question time in the colony's legislature, were aimed at China and at Tung Chee-hwa, a shipping billionaire who Beijing plans to install as Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader on July 1 when British rule ends.

The governor was responding to a question from Martin Lee, leader of the Democratic Party, on whether Britain would ask the United Nations Security Council to tackle China over Beijing's plan to disband Hong Kong's elected Legislative Council (Legco).
"Hong Kong is a very successful society... To borrow an analogy, it is a Rolls-Royce of a society," Patten told Legco.

He did not directly answer Lee's question, but said people could not understand why Tung and his team, along with Chinese officials, wanted to meddle with a system that has made Hong Kong one of the world's richest cities.

They "seem to want to examine the engine, tinker with the tyres rather than just turn on the ignition and drive the Rolls-Royce as successfully into the future as it has been driven in the past," Patten said.
"I think that causes genuine incomprehension elsewhere as well as genuine concerns," he said.
A leading human rights watchdog added its voice to the growing chorus of international criticism of China's plans.
"Freedom of association and freedom of assembly are fundamental rights under international law," Sidney Jones, head of U.S.-based Human Rights Watch/Asia, said in a statement.
China's plans "contradict efforts to make local laws fully compatible with international human rights standards", she said.
Hong Kong, a colony for over 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 with Tung as the Chief Executive of what will be an autonomous capitalist zone of China.

China has vowed the territory of 6.4 million people can keep its capitalistic way of life for a further 50 years. But China's appointment of a new legislature and its plan to roll back civil liberties and democracy has caused nervousness in Hong Kong.
The Democratic Party's Lee urged Patten to press London to take the legislature issue to the Security Council.
He said the council should force China to go to the world court for a ruling on the provisional legislature's legality.

The provisional legislature, chosen by a 400-strong China- controlled committee, will replace the elected Legco at the stroke of midnight on June 30, terminating democratic reforms introduced by Patten in the final years of British rule.

China has already rejected a British proposal to let the International Court of Justice at The Hague give its view on the provisional legislature, which is not mentioned in the 1984 Sino-British treaty covering the handover of Hong Kong.
But Patten noted that not many Security Council members took world court rulings as binding.
"There are not actually all that many members of the Security Council which do accept the arbitration of the International Court of Justice," he said.
China's handpicked Preparatory Committee working on the handover is soon to devise fresh election rules for polls that will elect a new long-term legislature in 1998.

"I am sure that it should remain a priority for the United Kingdom in the conduct of its foreign affairs to ensure that there is the maximum international support for the survival of freedom and the rule of law in Hong Kong," he said.
